When evaluating the performance of a locally hosted large language model, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct throughput metrics: prompt throughput and generation throughput. Prompt throughput measures the number of tokens processed per second during the inference phase where the model reads the input context. This metric is heavily influenced by the hardware’s memory bandwidth and the efficiency of the attention mechanism, as the model must compute attention scores for every token in the prompt. Generation throughput, on the other hand, measures the speed at which the model produces new tokens one by one. This phase is typically constrained by compute-bound operations, particularly matrix multiplications, and is often the bottleneck for user-perceived latency. Understanding the difference is critical because a model might excel at processing long prompts but struggle with rapid token generation, or vice versa, depending on the underlying hardware architecture.

A common pitfall in benchmarking is relying on very short outputs to gauge performance. When the expected output length is minimal, the overhead of model loading, context initialization, and the first few token generations dominates the total time. This skews the measured throughput upward, giving a false impression of high performance. For instance, a model that generates a single word may appear to have an astronomical tokens-per-second rate, but this figure is meaningless for real-world applications where users expect coherent, multi-sentence responses. To obtain accurate measurements, benchmarks should use prompts that elicit outputs of at least 100 to 200 tokens, ensuring that the generation phase is sufficiently sampled to reflect true sustained performance.

Comparing CPU-only, GPU-only, and hybrid runs requires careful consideration of the model’s size and the specific hardware capabilities. CPU-only inference is generally viable for smaller models, such as those with fewer than 7 billion parameters, especially when using optimized libraries like llama.cpp with quantization. However, as model size increases, the lack of parallel processing power on CPUs becomes a significant limitation, leading to sluggish generation speeds. GPU-only inference leverages the massive parallelism of graphics processors, dramatically accelerating both prompt processing and token generation. This is the preferred approach for larger models, provided the GPU has sufficient VRAM to hold the model weights and activation states. Hybrid runs, where parts of the model are offloaded to the GPU and the rest remain on the CPU, can offer a middle ground when VRAM is limited. However, hybrid setups often suffer from data transfer bottlenecks between the CPU and GPU, which can negate the benefits of partial offloading. Therefore, when comparing these configurations, it is important to normalize for model size and quantization level, and to report both prompt and generation throughput separately to provide a comprehensive view of performance.

In summary, interpreting local LLM throughput measurements demands a nuanced approach that accounts for the distinct characteristics of prompt and generation phases, avoids the distortion caused by short outputs, and carefully contextualizes hardware-specific performance differences. By adhering to these principles, practitioners can make informed decisions about model deployment and hardware selection, ensuring that their local LLMs deliver the expected performance in real-world scenarios.
